SK1103 Both branches end with the same statements

The if and the else block end with the same run of statements, so the shared tail is written twice and can drift apart in one place only.

CategoryModernization
Default severityhint
ScopeSyntax
Needs a compilationno
Runs under --load=looseyes
Cached per fileyes
Fixyes, review it
Language version floor—
Since2.0
ReSharperExtractCommonBranchingCode (resharper_extract_common_branching_code_highlighting)

Why

Duplication inside one member is where it is least visible and most likely to drift, because the two copies sit close enough to look like one. Moving the shared tail below the if states it once and leaves each branch holding only what actually differs. ⚠ An early jump inside a branch is safe, and working that out is what let the rule ship. The worry is if (c) { if (d) break; Log(); } else { Other(); Log(); } — the hoisted Log() looks as though it becomes reachable on the break path. It does not: the statement lands directly after the if, and every control transfer that skipped it inside the branch — return, throw, break, continue, goto, yield break — skips the position after the if exactly as it skipped the position before it. That is why no jump appears in the guards. ⚠ Nothing in the .NET SDK reports the shape, measured on the same net10.0 probe: shared trailing statements in if/else drew only CA1822, CA1002 and CA1062.

Example

Instead of:

if (retry) {
    Delay();
    Send(request);
} else {
    Prepare();
    Send(request);
}

Write:

if (retry) {
    Delay();
} else {
    Prepare();
}

Send(request);

When it does not fire

⚠ The leading half of the issue is refuted rather than narrowed, and the reason is evaluation order. A shared statement at the top of both branches can only be hoisted above the if, where it would run before the condition is evaluated instead of after it. if (Advance()) { Log(); … } else { Log(); … } and Log(); if (Advance()) … are different programs whenever the condition or the shared statement can observe the other, and deciding that requires purity analysis of two arbitrary expressions. The trailing half has no such problem, because the destination is immediately after the if and nothing is reordered relative to anything. ⚠ What the guards are about is names. A statement moved out of a branch leaves that branch's scope, so anything it names which the branch declared stops binding, and anything it declares moves outwards into the enclosing block — the scope move C# answers with CS0136. Every name either block declares anywhere is collected, and a mention of one of them in the moved statements withdraws the finding; so does the moved run declaring anything itself. It over-bails, counting names in a branch's own nested lambda that could never conflict, and over-bailing costs findings where the alternative costs builds. ⚠ The whole shared run is one finding, because reporting the last statement alone would fire again on the next one after its own fix. Both branches must be blocks and must keep at least one statement — a branch consumed entirely is a finding about the condition rather than about the tail — and the if itself must sit in a statement list, which excludes every arm of an else if chain because there is nowhere after it to put the moved statements. Structural equivalence ignores trivia, so a comment anywhere in either copy of the tail withdraws the finding: one copy is deleted and the other written back, and either duplicating a comment or losing it is a fix nobody can review. The fix is not marked safe — it changes the shape of a member and wants an eye on it. Generated code is excluded.
